einzeiler: The life and political legacy of China's powerful Empress Dowager Cixi
kurzfassung: Empress Dowager Cixi effectively ruled China for nearly fifty years during a period of immense upheaval, foreign invasion, and internal rebellion. Historians discuss her complex role in modernizing the Qing dynasty, balancing conservative traditions with political survival. Despite facing criticism for military defeats and power concentration, she remains a fascinating figure in Chinese history.
stichpunkte: Cixi rose from a low-ranking Manchu consort to become the dominant political figure behind the Qing throne.
The 19th century brought severe crises to China, notably the Opium Wars and the devastating Taiping Rebellion.
To combat internal revolts, the Qing government was forced to decentralize military power to regional leaders.
Japan's Meiji Restoration provided a successful model of rapid modernization that contrasted with China's struggles.
Cixi supported various self-strengthening reforms and naval development, though corruption hampered their success.
Her fateful decision to support the Boxer Rebellion led to foreign occupation and crippling financial indemnities.
In her final years, she finally implemented sweeping educational and constitutional reforms, though too late to save the dynasty.

beschreibung:
Misha Glenny delves in to the In Our Time archive to select ten episodes for listeners to revisit. His fifth choice, first released in May 2024, is the Empress Dowager Cixi, the woman who, for almost fifty years, was the most powerful figure in the Chinese court. Cixi (1835-1908) started out at court as one of the Emperor's many concubines, yet was the only one who gave him a son to succeed him and who also possessed great political skill and ambition. When their son became emperor he was still a young child and Cixi ruled first through him and then, following his death, through another child emperor. This was a time of rapid change in China, when western powers and Japan humiliated the forces of the Qing empire time after time, and Cixi had the chance to push forward the modernising reforms the country needed to thrive. However, when she found those reforms conflicted with her own interests or those of the Qing dynasty, she was arguably obstructive or too slow to act and she has been personally blamed for some of those many humiliations even when the fault lay elsewhere.
